raw.text: Milk is usually a white liquid food produced by the mammary glands of lactating mammals. It is the primary source of nutrition for young mammals before they are able to digest solid food. Milk contains many nutrients, including calcium and protein, as well as lactose and saturated fat; the enzyme lactase is needed to break down lactose. Immune factors and immune-modulating components in milk contribute to milk immunity. The first milk, which is called colostrum, contains antibodies and immune-modulating components that strengthen the immune system against many diseases.

certified.text: Raw milk or unpasteurized milk is milk that has not undergone pasteurization, a process of heating foods to kill pathogens for safe consumption and extension of shelf life.

homogenised.text: Milk pumped at high pressure through a narrow gap, which breaks its fat globules so small that they stay spread through it instead of rising as a layer of cream. Homogenised milk is also whiter and tastes fuller.

pasteurised.text: Milk heated briefly to kill the bacteria that make people ill and spoil it, usually to about 72 °C for 15 seconds, and cooled again at once. It is named after Louis Pasteur, who showed in the 1860s that gentle heating kept wine and beer from souring.

fresh.text: Pasteurised whole milk with its full fat, at least 3.5 % in the EU, chilled and keeping about a week unopened in the fridge. In Germany it is sold as Frischmilch, as against the longer-keeping ESL and UHT milks.

esl.text: Extended shelf life milk: heated higher than pasteurised milk, to about 125–130 °C for a second or two, or filtered through fine membranes, so that unopened in the fridge it keeps for about three weeks while tasting close to fresh milk.

uht.text: Ultra-high temperature processing (UHT), ultra-heat treatment, or ultra-pasteurization is a food processing technology that sterilizes liquid food by heating it above 140 °C (284 °F) – the temperature required to kill bacterial endospores – for two to five seconds. UHT is most commonly used in milk production, but the process is also used for fruit juices, cream, soy milk, yogurt, wine, soups, honey, and stews. UHT milk was first developed in the 1960s and became generally available for consumption in the 1970s. The heat used during the UHT process can cause Maillard browning and change the taste and smell of dairy products. An alternative process is flash pasteurization, in which the milk is heated to 72 °C (162 °F) for at least fifteen seconds.

sterilised.text: Milk heated in its sealed bottle or can to around 110–120 °C for 20 minutes or more, which kills everything in it and lets it keep for months unopened without cooling. The long heating browns it slightly and gives it a cooked, caramel taste.

evaporated.text: Evaporated milk, known in some countries as "unsweetened condensed milk", is a shelf-stable canned cow’s milk product, consisting of fresh milk from which approximately 60% of the water has been removed. French inventor Nicolas Appert, the "father of food science", perfected the process in the 1820s. It differs from sweetened condensed milk, which contains added sugar and requires less processing to preserve, as the added sugar inhibits bacterial growth. The production process involves the evaporation of 60% of the water from the milk, followed by homogenization, canning and heat sterilization.

condensed.text: Condensed milk is cow's milk from which water has been removed. It is most often found with sugar added, in the form of sweetened condensed milk, to the extent that the terms "condensed milk" and "sweetened condensed milk" are often used interchangeably today. Sweetened condensed milk is a very thick, sweet product, which when canned can last for years without refrigeration if not opened. The product is used in numerous dessert dishes in many countries.

milkPowder.text: Powdered milk, also called milk powder, dried milk, dry milk, or milk solids, is a manufactured dairy product made by evaporating milk to a state of dryness. One purpose of drying milk is to preserve it; milk powder has a far longer shelf life than liquid milk and does not need to be refrigerated, due to its low moisture content. Another purpose is to reduce its bulk for the economy of transportation. Powdered milk and dairy products include such items as dry whole milk, nonfat (skimmed) dry milk, dry buttermilk, dry whey products and dry dairy blends. Many exported dairy products conform to standards laid out in Codex Alimentarius.

bakedMilk.text: Baked milk is a variety of boiled milk that has been particularly popular in Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. It is made by simmering milk on low heat for eight hours or longer.

skimRaw.text: Raw milk with some or all of its cream taken off, once by letting it rise and skimming it by hand, now by spinning it off in a centrifugal separator. What is left is the starting point for semi-skimmed and skimmed milk.

semi.text: Milk with part of its fat taken out: in the EU it must have between 1.5 and 1.8 % fat, against at least 3.5 % for whole milk and no more than 0.5 % for skimmed.

semiUht.text: Semi-skimmed milk heated to 135–150 °C for a few seconds and packed sterile, so that it keeps for months unopened without a fridge. Sold in Germany as fettarme H-Milch.

semiEvaporated.text: Semi-skimmed milk with more than half its water evaporated off under low pressure, then canned and sterilised; in Germany it has between 1 and 7.5 % fat. Used in coffee and for cooking.

skimmed.text: Skimmed milk, or skim milk, is made when all the milkfat is removed from whole milk. It tends to contain around 0.1% to 0.3% fat.

skimmedEvaporated.text: Skimmed milk with more than half its water evaporated off and sterilised in the can, with no more than 1 % fat; used in coffee and for cooking.

skimmedPowder.text: Skimmed milk dried, mostly by spraying it into hot air, to a fine powder with no more than 1.5 % fat, which keeps for up to three years if stored cool and dry. Used in bread and cakes, confectionery and infant formula, and mixed back with water as milk where fresh milk is scarce.

colostrum.text: Colostrum, also known as foremilk, is the milk expressed by the mammary glands of a female mammal during the first few days following delivery of the newborn. Animal colostrum may be called beestings, the traditional word from Old English dialects.

colostrumPudding.text: A Swedish baked pudding (kalvdans) made from colostrum, the first milk a cow gives after calving. The colostrum is seasoned with sugar, salt and usually cinnamon or cardamom, then baked in a water bath until it sets. It is eaten warm or cold with jam, or sliced and fried.

colostrumPowder.text: Cow's colostrum, the first milk after calving, pasteurised at a low temperature and spray- or freeze-dried to a powder, kept gentle so as not to destroy its antibodies. Sold as a supplement for its immunoglobulins and growth factors.

travelan.text: Colostrum from pregnant cows vaccinated against the strains of E. coli that cause traveller's diarrhoea, so that their first milk is full of antibodies against them. Freeze-dried to a powder and pressed into tablets, sold as Travelan; a large trial in 2025 found it gave little protection.
travelan.sourceName: Otto et al., Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology (2011)

milkDrugs.text: Human proteins made in the milk of genetically modified animals and purified from it as medicines. The first approved was ATryn, an anticoagulant from goats' milk (2006); Ruconest, for hereditary angioedema, is made in rabbits' milk.

rawCream.text: The fat-rich part of raw milk, skimmed off as it rises or spun off in a separator, usually at 35–40 % fat. Pasteurised, standardised and soured, it becomes all the creams.

cream.text: Cream is a dairy product composed of the higher-fat layer skimmed from the top of milk before homogenization. The butterfat, which is less dense, rises to the top and is skimmed off, resulting in gravity cream. The industrial production of cream instead uses centrifugal separators to make separator cream. Cream is often sold in grades defined by their butterfat content. It contains high levels of saturated fat, in ascending proportion from light cream to heavy cream.

clotted.text: Clotted cream is a thick cream made by heating full-cream cow's milk using steam or a water bath and then leaving it in shallow pans to cool slowly. During this time, the cream content rises to the surface and forms "clots" or "clouts", hence the name. Clotted cream is an essential ingredient for cream tea.

rabri.text: Rabri, rabdi or rabidi is a sweet, condensed-milk-based dish, originating from the Indian subcontinent, made by boiling milk on low heat for a long time until it becomes dense and changes its colour to off-white or pale yellow. Jaggery, spices, and nuts are added to it to give it flavor. It is chilled and served as dessert. Rabri is the main ingredient in several desserts, such as rasabali, chhena kheeri, and khira sagara.

creamGrades.text: Cream as it is sold: the cream spun off raw milk, its fat set to a grade, by adding back skimmed milk, and then pasteurised or UHT-treated. Each country names its own grades by how much fat they have, from coffee cream to double cream.

kaffeeobers.text: Austria’s coffee cream: cream of at least 10 % fat, to which nothing is added when it is pasteurised.

halfAndHalf.text: A mixture of milk and cream with at least 10.5 % and less than 18 % milkfat, poured into coffee in the United States.

singleCream.text: Britain’s pouring cream, with at least 18 % fat: too lean to whip, used in coffee and over puddings.

lightCream.text: Cream with at least 18 % and less than 30 % milkfat, also sold in the United States as coffee cream or table cream.

schlagsahne.text: German whipping cream: at least 30 % fat, and it must whip; its protein may not be raised by adding any.

schlagobers.text: Austria’s whipping cream: at least 30 % fat, or 36 % sold as “extra schlagfähig”, extra whippable.

heavyCream.text: Cream with at least 36 % milkfat, the richest of the creams defined in the United States, often sold as heavy whipping cream.

cremeDouble.text: A particularly rich sweet cream of 40 to 55 % fat, firm enough to spoon and to cook with without splitting, used to finish soups, sauces and desserts.

coffeeCream.text: Cream standardised to at least 10 % fat, usually 10–15 %, homogenised and UHT-treated or sterilised so that it keeps and stays smooth in hot coffee. Sold in Germany as Kaffeesahne.

cremeDeLeite.text: Brazil’s cream, sold above all in cans and UHT cartons that keep without cooling, and stirred into strogonoff and desserts; by law it has at least 10 % fat.

namaKurimu.text: Japan’s “fresh cream”: what the milk ordinance calls cream, at least 18 % fat with nothing added. Cream with emulsifiers, stabilisers or vegetable fat in it is not cream there, and much of what is sold for whipping is.

mediaCrema.text: Mexico’s “half cream”: a sweet table cream of about 20 % fat, sold in small cans that keep, and spooned over fruit, soups and enchiladas.

pannaDaCucina.text: Italy’s cooking cream: UHT cream of at least 20 % fat, too lean and too processed to whip, kept in the cupboard for sauces; the cream for whipping has at least 30 %.
pannaDaCucina.sourceName: Il Fatto Alimentare: panna da cucina

thickenedCream.text: Australia’s everyday cream: at least 35 % fat, as all cream there must have, with gelatine or another thickener added so that it whips firmer and holds.

vispgradde.text: Sweden’s whipping cream, at 40 % fat richer than most countries’, with nothing in it but pasteurised cream.

cremeLegere.text: France’s light cream: at least 12 % and less than 30 % fat, poured or thickened, as the full crème has at least 30 %.
cremeLegere.sourceName: French Ministry of the Economy: laits et crèmes

kaffeerahm.text: Switzerland’s coffee cream: UHT-treated cream with at least 15 % milk fat, sold in the small portion cups that go with coffee.
kaffeerahm.sourceName: Swissmilk: Crème fraîche, Kaffeerahm und Co.

cremeFluide.text: France’s plain cream, at least 30 % fat: sold as crème fraîche fluide when it is only pasteurised, for in France crème fraîche need not be soured; only the épaisse, thick, kind is.
cremeFluide.sourceName: French Ministry of the Economy: laits et crèmes

vollrahm.text: Switzerland’s full cream for whipping, at least 35 % fat, more than the 30 % of German Schlagsahne.

doppelrahm.text: Switzerland’s double cream, at least 45 % fat, thick enough to spoon; the double crème of the Gruyère is eaten with meringues.
doppelrahm.sourceName: Swissmilk: Crème fraîche, Kaffeerahm und Co.

saurerHalbrahm.text: Switzerland’s lighter soured cream, at least 15 % fat; its full soured cream is sold as crème fraîche, at least 35 %.
saurerHalbrahm.sourceName: Swissmilk: Crème fraîche, Kaffeerahm und Co.

whipping.text: Britain’s whipping cream: at least 35 % fat, enough to trap air when beaten and hold it as whipped cream.

double.text: British cream with at least 48 % fat, the richest after clotted cream: thick enough to spoon, it whips easily and can go into hot sauces without splitting.

evaporatedCream.text: Milk or cream concentrated by evaporation to at least 15 % fat and sterilised in the can or bottle, so that it keeps without cooling; the richest grade of condensed milk, sold in Germany for coffee as Kondenssahne or kondensierte Kaffeesahne.

culturedCream.text: Cream soured with lactic acid bacteria, which thicken it and give it its tang. It is one product under many names, from Saure Sahne to crème fraîche, told apart by little more than how much fat the cream has.

saureSahne.text: Germany’s everyday soured cream, sold as Saure Sahne or Sauerrahm: cream soured with lactic acid bacteria to at least 10 % fat, and not heated again after souring.

sauerrahm.text: Austria’s soured cream: made as sour milk is, but from cream of at least 10 % fat, and mostly from cream of 15 %, the fat it is usually sold at.

smetana.text: Smetana is the English-language name for the different types of sour cream traditionally prevalent in Central, Eastern, and Southeastern Europe, and Central Asia. It is a dairy product produced by souring heavy cream. It is similar to crème fraîche, but nowadays mainly sold with 9% to 42% milkfat content depending on the country. Its cooking properties are different from crème fraîche and sour cream sold in the US, which contain 18% butterfat. It is widely used in cooking and baking.

graddfil.text: Sweden’s soured cream: cream of usually 12 % fat, homogenised, pasteurised and then soured with a culture. It was first tried in Sweden as “sur grädde”, a word-for-word translation of the English sour cream.

tejfol.text: Hungary’s soured cream, bone-white, thick and pourable: by the Hungarian food code, cream made from milk with added cream or butter, homogenised and set by a pure culture of lactic acid bacteria.

sourCream.text: Sour cream is a dairy product obtained by fermenting regular cream with certain kinds of lactic acid bacteria. The bacterial culture, which is introduced either deliberately or naturally, sours and thickens the cream. Its name comes from the production of lactic acid by bacterial fermentation, which is called souring.

schmand.text: Schmand is cream soured with lactic acid bacteria to between 15 and 25 % fat: thicker and richer than sour cream, leaner than crème fraîche, and, unlike them, it may be heated again after souring, which helps it keep. Further east the same thing is smetana.

cremeFraiche.text: Crème fraîche is a dairy product similar to sour cream; it is a soured cream containing 10–45% butterfat, with a pH of approximately 4.5. It is soured with a bacterial culture. European labeling regulations specify the two ingredients must be cream and bacterial culture. It is served over fruit and baked goods, as well as being added to soups and sauces. It is used in a variety of other recipes. Sour cream is a similar foodstuff, except that crème fraîche is less sour and has a higher fat content. Sour cream may contain thickening agents not permitted in crème fraîche in many jurisdictions.

mascarpone.text: Mascarpone is a soft Italian dairy product obtained by acid-heat coagulation of cream. It is a dairy cream, not a cheese in the technical sense, as it is made without rennet and does not undergo true curd formation. It is recognized as a prodotto agroalimentare tradizionale (PAT).

posset.text: A posset, was originally a popular hot drink made of milk curdled with wine or ale, often spiced, which was often used as a remedy. In the 18th century, it was reportedly only drunk in Sweden, Norway and England.

junket.text: Junket is a milk-based dessert with a jelly texture, made with sweetened milk and rennet, the digestive enzyme that curdles milk. It is usually set in a mould and served cold.

gomme.text: Gomme is a traditional Norwegian dish usually served as a spread or a dessert. Gomme has long traditions in several places in the country and was largely used as a party food when cakes were served, for example at Christmas.

iceCream.text: Ice cream is a frozen dessert typically made from milk or cream that has been flavoured with a sweetener, either sugar or an alternative, and a spice, such as cocoa or vanilla, or with fruit, such as strawberries or peaches. Food colouring is sometimes added in addition to stabilizers. The mixture is cooled below the freezing point of water and stirred to incorporate air spaces and prevent detectable ice crystals from forming. It can also be made by whisking a flavoured cream base and liquid nitrogen together. The result is a smooth, semi-solid foam that is solid at very low temperatures. It becomes more malleable as its temperature increases.

kulfi.text: Kulfi is a frozen dairy dessert from the Indian subcontinent. It is often described as "traditional Indian ice cream". Kulfi originated in 16th-century Delhi during the Mughal era.

butter.text: Butter is a dairy product made from the fat and protein components of churned cream. It is a semi-solid emulsion at room temperature, consisting of approximately 81% butterfat. It is used at room temperature as a spread, melted as a condiment, and used as a fat in baking, sauce-making, pan frying, and other cooking procedures.

culturedButter.text: Butter churned from cream that has first been soured with lactic acid bacteria, giving it a fuller, slightly tangy taste and the aroma of diacetyl. Sold in Germany as Sauerrahmbutter.

mildButter.text: Butter churned from sweet cream, with an aromatic culture and a concentrate of lactic acid worked into it afterwards. This Dutch method, from the dairy institute NIZO, gives a cultured aroma without souring the cream and leaves a sweet buttermilk. Sold in Germany as mildgesäuerte Butter.

butterfat.text: Ghee is a type of clarified butter, originating in the Indian Subcontinent. It is a widely used butter for cooking especially in Indian cuisines and in Hindu religious rituals. Typically made from cow butter or buffalo butter, ghee is favoured for its nutty flavour and high smoke point allowing it to be heated at high temperatures without burning.

clarified.text: Clarified butter is butter from which all milk solids have been removed. The result is a clear, yellow butter that can be heated to higher temperatures before burning.

amf.text: Pure milk fat, with at least 99.8 % fat and next to no water or milk solids, made by separating melted butter or cream and drying the oil under vacuum. Traded in drums as an industrial ingredient for chocolate, ice cream and recombined milk.

smen.text: Smen is a salted, fermented butter native to North African cuisine, as well as a traditional Yemeni dish. In countries like Jordan and Lebanon, samneh is a type of butter similar to clarified butter, while north African smen is a type of fermented butter similar to ghee.

bogButter.text: Bog butter is an ancient waxy substance found buried in peat bogs, particularly in Ireland and Scotland. Likely an old method of making and preserving butter, some tested lumps of bog butter were made of dairy, while others were made of animal fat.

nitirKibbeh.text: Niter kibbeh, or niter qibe, also called tesmi, is a seasoned, clarified butter used in Ethiopian and Eritrean cuisine and of Indian origin. Its preparation is similar to that of ghee, but niter kibbeh is simmered with spices such as besobela, koseret, fenugreek, cumin, coriander, turmeric, Ethiopian cardamom (korarima), cinnamon, or nutmeg before straining, imparting a distinct, spicy aroma. The version using vegetable oil instead of butter is called yeqimem zeyet.

churn.text: The liquid left in the churn when cream turns to butter: thin and low in fat, with most of the cream's other milk solids still in it. Sold sweet, or soured with a culture as buttermilk; in Germany buttermilk may have no more than 1 % fat.

buttermilk.text: Buttermilk is a dairy drink made by adding lactic acid bacteria to milk to produce a fermented dairy drink. Traditionally, it was made from the nearly fat-free milk remaining after churning butter from cream, which was cultured with natural bacteria prior to and during churning, giving a slight sour taste to the buttermilk and preventing spoilage. However, with the ubiquity of refrigeration in industrialized countries, butter in those areas is typically made from uncultured or "sweet" cream. Therefore, most modern buttermilk is specifically produced by inoculating fresh, pasteurized milk, and is available in different levels of fat content.

fermButtermilk.text: What is left when butter is churned from whole milk that has first been soured, rather than from cream: from dahi in South Asia, from ergo in Ethiopia and from soured milk in the Maghreb. A thin, sour drink, known as chaas or mattha in India and lben in Morocco.
fermButtermilk.sourceName: Journal of Food Science and Technology (2020)

soured.text: Soured milk, sour milk, spontaneously soured milk, or naturally soured milk is the milk product fermented with indigenous microorganisms, as opposed to cultured milk of which the production involves controlled fermentation with starter cultures. Lactic acid produced by the bacteria causes milk to coagulate and thicken, inhibiting the growth of harmful bacteria and improving the product's shelf life.

ropy.text: A Scandinavian type of fermented milk with a stringy, slimy ('ropy') texture. It is soured at room temperature by mesophilic Lactococcus lactis strains that give off exopolysaccharides, long sugar chains that form the slime. The Finnish viili is the best-studied example.

ryazhenka.text: Ryazhenka or ryazhanka, is a traditional fermented milk product in Ukraine, Russia, and Belarus. It is made from baked milk by lactic acid fermentation.

kefir.text: Kefir is a fermented milk drink similar to a thin yogurt or ayran that is made from kefir grains, a specific type of mesophilic symbiotic culture. It is prepared by inoculating the milk of cows, goats, or sheep with kefir grains.

mildYoghurt.text: Yoghurt made with milder-souring cultures, often Lactobacillus acidophilus and bifidobacteria, in place of the usual Lactobacillus bulgaricus, and often sold for its probiotic bacteria. Less sour than ordinary yoghurt; in Germany sold as Joghurt mild.

probioticDrink.text: Milk fermented with a single strain of probiotic bacteria rather than with yoghurt cultures, such as acidophilus milk, made with Lactobacillus acidophilus, or Yakult, a small sweetened drink of skimmed milk fermented with Lactobacillus casei Shirota since 1935.

yoghurt.text: Yogurt, also spelled yoghurt, is a food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk. The bacteria ferment the sugars in the milk and produce lactic acid, which acts on milk protein to give yogurt its texture and characteristic tart flavor. Yogurt is most commonly made from cow's milk, but milk from water buffalo, goats, ewes, mares, camels, and yaks can also be used.

mishtiDoi.text: Mishti doi is a fermented sweet doi (curd) originating from the Bengal region of the Indian subcontinent. It is popular in Bangladesh and in the Indian states of West Bengal, Tripura, Assam's Barak Valley. It is made with milk and sugar or jaggery. It differs from plain yogurt because of the technique of preparation. There are many variations of mishti doi according to their popularity. Sweet curd of Nabadwip, Kolkata, Bogra, etc are very popular.

creamYoghurt.text: Yoghurt made from cream with the usual yoghurt cultures, to at least 10 % fat. Sold in Germany as Sahnejoghurt.

greek.text: Strained yogurt, Labneh, Greek or Greek-style yogurt, yogurt cheese, sack yogurt, hung curd, or kerned yogurt is yogurt that has been strained to remove most of its whey, making it thicker while preserving its sour taste. In Europe and North America, it is often made from low-fat or fat-free cow's milk. In Iceland a similar product named skyr is made. Labneh is a strained yogurt thicker than Greek yogurt.

skyr.text: Skyr is a traditional Icelandic cultured dairy product. It has the consistency of strained yogurt, but a milder flavor. Skyr can be classified as a fresh sour milk cheese, similar to curd cheese consumed like a yogurt in the Baltic states, the Low Countries and Germany. It has been a part of Icelandic cuisine for centuries.

ayran.text: Ayran is a cold savory yogurt-based beverage found throughout Central Asia, the Balkans, and the Middle East. The drink is a heterogeneous mixture that has been consumed by Turkic peoples for approximately 1,000 years. The principal ingredients are yogurt, water and salt. Herbs such as mint may be added, and some varieties are carbonated. It is a national drink of Turkey and is served in most restaurants in Bulgaria.

driedYoghurt.text: Strained yoghurt, buttermilk or soured milk, shaped and dried until hard: a family of keeping foods of Iran, the Caucasus and Central Asia, rolled into balls, sliced into strips or formed into chunks.

kishk.text: A dried fermented food made from milk or yogurt and cereal, usually bulgur, and also known as tarhana or burghul yoghurt. It has been eaten for centuries across the Middle East, western Asia and parts of Africa. The cereal adds nutrients that milk lacks, and some versions include vegetables or spices.

qaraqurut.text: A black, highly acidic dairy product of Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia, made by boiling down the sour whey left from making kashk, or qurut, until it thickens, then drying it until brittle.
qaraqurut.sourceName: Wikipedia: Qaraqorut (citing Walker, Milk – Beyond the Dairy, 1999)

dadiah.text: Dadiah (Minangkabau) or dadih is a traditional fermented milk popular among people of West Sumatra, Indonesia. It is made by pouring fresh, raw, unheated, buffalo milk into a bamboo tube capped with a banana leaf and allowing it to ferment spontaneously at room temperature for two days.

mursik.text: Mursik is a traditional fermented milk variant of the Kalenjin people of Kenya. It can be made from cow or goat milk and is fermented in a specially made calabash gourd locally known as a sotet. The gourd is lined with soot from specific trees, such as the African senna, which add flavor to the fermented milk. It is normally consumed with ugali or on its own and is served at room temperature or chilled.

choormog.text: Camel's milk soured into a slightly acidic, sometimes fizzy and faintly alcoholic drink wherever camels are herded: shubat in Kazakhstan, chal in Turkmenistan, khoormog in Mongolia, gariss in Sudan and suusac in northern Kenya.

kumis.text: Kumis, alternatively spelled coumis or kumyz, also known as airag, is a traditional fermented dairy product made from mare milk. The drink is important to the peoples of the Central and East Asian steppes, of Turkic and Mongolic origin: Volga Tatars, Kazakhs, Bashkirs, Kalmyks, Kyrgyz, Siberian Tatars, Mongols, and Yakuts. Kumis was also historically consumed by the Magyars as well as the Khitans, Jurchens, and Han of northern China.

arkhi.text: Arkhi is a liquor made from airag, fermented milk brandy, or isgelen tarag which then gets distilled. Isgelen tarag often uses the milk of a mare, donkeys, sheep, cows, the yak, camels or of reindeer, depending on local traditions or availability. The Mongols adopted the distillation technology from Arab and Islamic producers of arak, a grape-based spirit, substituting their own local fermented ingredients to distill sometime in the 13th century. Their transmission of this technology to Korea led to the production of Soju there.

arkhiGrades.text: Arkhi distilled again to make it stronger. In Mongolian the grades have their own names: arz is arkhi distilled a second time and khorz is arz distilled once more, and a proverb warns that distilling khorz again gives khor, poison.

stillCheese.text: What is left in the pot after soured milk has been distilled into milk spirit. Kalmyks call it bozo and press it into a curd, aadmag, which is made into dried cakes, or use it to dress hides; Mongolian herders dry the mash into aaruul.
stillCheese.sourceName: Stepnye Vesti (Kalmyk newspaper), 'O molochnoi pishche i napitkakh kalmykov'

curd.text: Curd is obtained by coagulating milk in a sequential process called curdling. It can be a final dairy product or the first stage in cheesemaking. The coagulation can be caused by adding rennet, a culture, or any edible acidic substance such as lemon juice or vinegar, and then allowing it to coagulate. The increased acidity causes the milk proteins (casein) to tangle into solid masses, or curds. Milk that has been left to sour will also automatically produce curds, and sour milk cheeses are produced this way.

quark.text: Quark or quarg is a type of fresh dairy product made from milk. The milk is soured, usually by adding lactic acid bacteria cultures, and strained once the desired curdling is achieved. It can be classified as fresh acid-set cheese. Traditional quark can be made without rennet, but in modern dairies small quantities of rennet are typically added. It is soft, white and unaged, and usually has no salt added.

sourMilkCheese.text: Acid-set or sour milk cheese is cheese that has been curdled (coagulated) by natural souring, often from lactic acid bacteria, or by the addition of acid. This type of cheese is technologically simple to produce.

cookedCheese.text: A spreadable German cheese made from drained quark. Baking soda is mixed in and left to work until the curd turns glassy, and the curd is then gently heated and stirred until it melts. Butter, salt and often caraway are added. Industrial versions use melting salts. It is closely related to French cancoillotte.

mish.text: An Egyptian cheese made by fermenting salted soft cheese, traditionally Areesh, for a year or more in an earthenware jar under a pickle of buttermilk, sour milk, whey and peppers. It turns yellowish-brown, sharp and pungent. The jar can be topped up with fresh cheese for years.
mish.sourceName: Wikipedia (citing Robinson & Tamime, Feta and Related Cheeses, 1991)

eezgii.text: A Mongolian cheese of cow's, sheep's or goat's milk: the curd is boiled in its own whey until the whey has soaked in and cooked away, leaving it brown and lightly sweet. It is dried on racks and stored for the winter.
eezgii.sourceName: ICH Links (ICHCAP/UNESCO intangible heritage archive), 'Making of Eezgii'

rushan.text: Rushan is a cow's milk cheese of Yunnan, China. It is traditionally made by the Bai people, who call it nvxseiz, the etymology of which is unclear.

chhena.text: Chhena ଛେନ୍ନା in Odia or chhana ছানা in Bengali, is a kind of acid-set cheese originating in the Indian subcontinent that is made from water buffalo or cow milk by adding food acids such as lemon juice and calcium lactate instead of rennet and straining out the whey.

paneer.text: Paneer is a fresh acid-set cheese, common in South Asian cuisine, made from cow milk or buffalo milk. It is a non-aged, non-melting soft cheese made by curdling milk with an acid, such as lemon juice or citric acid. Paneer is predominantly used in north Indian dishes and is commonly used throughout South Asia, especially India, due to its versatility as an ingredient in diverse dishes.

chhenaSweets.text: The sweets of eastern India and Bangladesh made from chhena kneaded smooth: rolled into balls and cooked in syrup as rasgulla, soaked in sweetened, thickened milk as rasmalai, or cooked with sugar and shaped as sandesh.

plantCheese.text: Cheese set not by rennet from a calf's stomach or by acid but by an enzyme from a plant: cardoon thistle flowers in the cheeses of Portugal and Spain, Calotropis in West Africa's wagashi, papaya latex in Indonesia's dangke, ginger juice in southern China's ginger milk curd.
plantCheese.sourceName: Heliyon (2022), Processing and preservation methods of Wagashi Gassirè

rennetCurd.text: Milk set into a soft gel by rennet, an extract of calves' stomachs whose working enzyme is chymosin, or by a substitute enzyme: it turns casein into paracasein, which links into a network that traps the fat. Cut, stirred, heated, drained and pressed to different degrees, it becomes most cheeses.
rennetCurd.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Cheese

freshCheese.text: Cheese eaten young, with little or no ripening, so it stays soft, moist and mild and keeps only briefly: under German cheese law it holds more than 73 % water in the cheese without its fat. Set with rennet, as these are, or mainly with acid, as quark and cottage cheese are.

soft.text: Cheese that keeps much of its water, more than 67 % in the cheese without its fat under German cheese law, so that it stays soft and, as it ripens from the outside in, turns creamy. In Germany called Weichkäse; the bloomy and washed rinds are soft cheeses taken further.

semiHard.text: Cheese whose curd is pressed and ripened for about one to three months, firm enough to cut cleanly into slices: under German cheese law it holds more than 54 and up to 63 % water in the cheese without its fat. Germany calls it Schnittkäse, cheese for slicing; Gouda, Edam and Tilsiter are among them.

hard.text: Cheese whose curd is cut to the size of wheat grains, heated to around 50 °C and pressed, then ripened for three months to over three years, until it holds no more than 56 % water in the cheese without its fat. Emmentaler, Parmesan, Grana Padano and Pecorino are among them.

bloomy.text: Soft cheese ripened under a white rind of mould, Penicillium camemberti, whose enzymes break down its protein from the surface towards the centre, so that it softens from the outside in. Brie and Camembert are the classic examples.
bloomy.sourceName: Codex Alimentarius draft standard for Camembert (FAO)

blue.text: Blue cheese is any cheese made with the addition of cultures of edible molds, which create blue-green spots or veins through the cheese. Blue cheeses vary in flavor from mild to strong and from slightly sweet to salty or sharp; in color from pale to dark; and in consistency from liquid to hard. They may have a distinctive smell, either from the mold or from various specially cultivated bacteria such as Brevibacterium linens.

washed.text: Washed-rind or smear-ripened cheeses are cheeses which are periodically treated with brine or mold-bearing agents. This encourages the growth of certain bacteria on their surfaces which give them distinctive flavors. There are hard and soft washed-rind cheeses. The softer ones are sometimes distinguished as "smear-ripened". Conversely, the term "washed-rind" is sometimes reserved only for the hard ones.

alpine.text: Swiss-type cheeses, also known as Alpine cheeses, are a group of hard or semi-hard cheeses with a distinct character, whose origins lie in the Alps of Europe, although they are now eaten and imitated in most cheesemaking parts of the world. Their distinct character arose from the requirements of cheese made in the summer on high Alpine grasslands, and then transported with the cows down to the valleys in the winter, in the historic culture of Alpine transhumance. Traditionally the cheeses were made in large rounds or "wheels" with a hard rind, and were robust enough for both keeping and transporting.

cheddared.text: The manufacture of Cheddar cheese includes the process of cheddaring, which contributes significantly to the unique flavour profile of the eponymous cheese, but is employed in the production of many related and inspired varieties, such as Red Leicester and Lincolnshire Poacher. Cheddar cheese is named for the village of Cheddar in Somerset in Southwest England where it was originally manufactured. The technique applied in the production of this cheese has since spread around the world and thus the name of its most significant component — cheddaring — has become generically known.

washedCurd.text: Cheese whose curd has part of its whey drawn off and replaced with water while it is being made, diluting its milk sugar so that less lactic acid forms: the cheese ends up less acidic and smooth in texture. Gouda, Edam, Havarti and Tilsiter are made this way.
washedCurd.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Cheese

insect.text: Cheese ripened with the help of insects or mites: the larvae of the cheese fly, Piophila casei, that work through Sardinia's sheep's-milk casu marzu, or the mites put on the rinds of France's Mimolette and Germany's Milbenkäse, which help give them their rind and character.
insect.sourceName: Journal of Dairy Science (2010), Melnyk et al.

tulum.text: Tulum cheese is a traditional Turkish goat's milk cheese ripened in a goatskin casing, called tulum in Turkish.

processed.text: Processed cheese is a product made from cheese mixed with an emulsifying agent. Additional ingredients, such as unfermented dairy ingredients, salt, vegetable oils, sugar, or food coloring may be included. As a result, many flavors, colors, and textures of processed cheese exist. Processed cheese typically contains around 50–60% cheese and 40–50% other ingredients.

grilling.text: Cheese made with little or no acid and heated hard, boiled in its whey or baked, so that its protein network holds and it softens when grilled or fried instead of melting. Halloumi, cooked in whey at up to 90 °C, and Finland's leipäjuusto, baked or grilled after setting, are the best known.
grilling.sourceName: culture: the word on cheese, 'Squeaky, Non-Melting Cheeses'

pastaFilata.text: Stretch-curd cheeses are those prepared using the pasta filata technique. They are also known as pulled-curd and plastic-curd cheeses. The cheeses manufactured from this technique undergo a plasticising and kneading treatment of the fresh curd in hot water, which gives them fibrous structures.

stracciatella.text: Stracciatella is a fresh cheese originating from Apulia, Italy, made by shredding stretched curd and, traditionally, mixing it with cream. It may be produced from either cow's milk or Italian buffalo milk, depending on the mozzarella used.

bryndza.text: Bryndza or brynza is a sheep milk cheese made across the countries in Central and Eastern Europe, most notably in Slovakia and Poland. Bryndza cheese is creamy white in appearance, known for its characteristic strong smell and taste. The cheese is white, tangy, crumbly and slightly moist. It has characteristic odor and flavor with a notable taste of butyric acid. The overall flavor sensation begins slightly mild, then goes strong and finally fades to a salty finish. Recipes differ slightly across countries.

brined.text: Brined cheese, also sometimes referred to as pickled cheese for some varieties, is cheese that is matured in brine in an airtight or semi-permeable container. This process gives the cheese good stability, inhibiting bacterial growth even in warmer climates. Brined cheeses may be soft or hard, varying in moisture content and in colour and flavour according to the type of milk used. However, all are rindless and generally taste clean, salty and acidic when fresh, developing some piquancy when aged; most are white.

buttermilkCheese.text: Cheese made by heating the buttermilk left from churning soured milk until its proteins curdle, then draining the curd. The cheese of the Himalaya, Ethiopia and Anatolia: soft chhurpi, datshi, ayib and çökelek.
buttermilkCheese.sourceName: Food Science & Nutrition (2022), on Bhutanese datshi

hardChhurpi.text: Chhurpi, otherwise known as durkha and chogo/chugo, is a traditional cheese consumed in Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and parts of Northeastern India. The two varieties of chhurpi are a soft variety and a very hard variety. Chhurpi is considered one of the hardest cheeses in the world.

khoa.text: Khoa, khoya, khowa or mawa is a soft cheese widely used in South Asian cuisine, encompassing India, Nepal, and Pakistan. It is made of either dried whole milk or milk thickened by heating in an open iron pan. It is lower in moisture than typical fresh cheeses such as ricotta. It is made from whole milk instead of whey.

khoaSweets.text: Sweets made from khoa, milk boiled down in an open pan to a stiff dough: cooked with sugar into peda and burfi, or kneaded with flour, fried and soaked in syrup as gulab jamun.

dulce.text: Dulce de leche, caramelized milk, milk candy, or milk jam is a confection commonly made by heating sugar and milk over several hours. The substance takes on a spreadable, sauce-like consistency and derives its rich flavour and colour from non-enzymatic browning. It is typically used to top or fill other sweet foods.

sweetWhey.text: The whey that drains from curd set with rennet, in making most cheeses and rennet casein: only mildly acidic, at pH 5.9 to 6.6, and carrying the milk's sugar, its whey proteins and its minerals. About half of processed whey solids now go into whey protein concentrates, isolates, lactose and permeate.
sweetWhey.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Whey processing

acidWhey.text: The whey left after milk is curdled with acid instead of rennet, from fresh cheeses such as cottage cheese and quark, from Greek-style yogurt, or from acid casein. It has a pH of about 4.3–5, against roughly 6 for sweet whey, and is rich in calcium phosphate and lactic acid, which make it hard to dry.

wheyCream.text: The fat left in whey, spun off in a separator: a cream of usually 25–30 % fat, against about 40 % for milk cream. It can go back into the cheese milk, or be churned into whey butter.
wheyCream.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Whey processing

wheyButter.text: Butter churned from whey cream, the fat skimmed off cheese whey. Whey cream has 25–30% fat, less than ordinary cream. Cheesemakers turn it into butter when they would rather not return it to the cheese milk, for example because of the risk of bacteriophages.

wheyCheese.text: Brunost is a common Norwegian name for mysost, a family of soft cheese-related foods made with whey, milk, and/or cream. The characteristic brown color and sweet taste result from milk sugars being caramelized after boiling. The term brunost is often used to refer to fløtemysost or Gudbrandsdalsost, which are the most popular varieties.

prim.text: A soft, sweet, light golden-brown spread from Norway, called mysmør or prim there and messmör in Sweden. It is made by boiling down whey with cream, like brunost, but it is sweetened with sugar and left spreadable instead of being pressed into a block. It tastes of mild caramel.

ricotta.text: Ricotta is an Italian whey cheese made from sheep, cow, goat, or Italian water buffalo milk whey left over from the production of other cheeses. However, modern ricotta is often made from milk instead of whey. Like other whey cheeses, it is made by coagulating the proteins that remain after the casein has been used to make cheese, notably albumin and globulin.

blaand.text: Blaand, or bland is a fermented milk product made from whey. It is acidic and has very low alcohol content.

wheyPowder.text: Sweet whey concentrated and spray-dried to a powder, still holding its lactose, proteins and minerals. Used in bakery, soups and other processed foods, and in animal feed.
wheyPowder.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Milk and whey powder

wpc.text: Whey with much of its lactose and minerals filtered out through an ultrafiltration membrane that holds back the proteins, then dried: a powder of 35 to 80 % protein in its dry matter. Used in sports and clinical nutrition and in many foods.
wpc.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Whey processing

wpi.text: Whey protein separated further, by membrane filtration or ion exchange, to more than 90 % protein in its dry matter, with almost no fat or lactose left. Used in sports and clinical nutrition.
wpi.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Whey processing

permeate.text: What passes through the membrane when whey is ultrafiltered to make whey protein: water, lactose and the milk's minerals, with some acids, but no protein. Dried as an ingredient, or crystallised for its lactose.
permeate.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Milk and whey powder

lactose.text: Lactose is a disaccharide composed of galactose and glucose and has the molecular formula C12H22O11. Lactose makes up around 2–8% of milk (by mass). The name comes from lac (gen. lactis), the Latin word for milk, plus the suffix -ose used to name sugars. The compound is a white, water-soluble, non-hygroscopic solid with a mildly sweet taste. It is used in the food industry.

lactoseDerivatives.text: Galactooligosaccharides (GOS), also known as oligogalactosyllactose, oligogalactose, oligolactose or transgalactooligosaccharides (TOS), belong to the group of prebiotics. Prebiotics are defined as non-digestible food ingredients that beneficially affect the host by stimulating the growth and/or activity of beneficial bacteria in the colon. GOS occurs in commercially available products such as food for both infants and adults.

lactulose.text: Lactulose is a non-absorbable sugar used in the treatment of constipation and hepatic encephalopathy. It is administered orally for constipation, and either orally or rectally for hepatic encephalopathy. It generally begins working after 8–12 hours, but may take up to 2 days to improve constipation.

inhalers.text: A dry-powder inhaler (DPI) is a device that delivers medication to the lungs in the form of a dry powder. DPIs are commonly used to treat respiratory diseases such as asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, and COPD, although DPIs have also been used in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.

lactoferrin.text: Lactoferrin (LF), also known as lactotransferrin (LTF), is a multifunctional protein found in milk and mucus which is encoded by the LTF gene in humans. It functions as an antimicrobial protein and affects the body's immune response in a complex way, with both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects.

glycomacropeptide.text: Glycomacropeptide (GMP) is a glycosylated peptide formed during renneting as a fragment of sweet whey. Acid whey from yogurt or curdling cheese without the use of rennet does not contain GMP. The unglycosylated form is known as caseinomacropeptide or CMP. Both forms exist in roughly similar amounts in whey.

blotto.text: Bovine Lacto Transfer Technique Optimizer: a solution of nonfat dry milk, usually 5 % in buffer, used in laboratories since 1984 to block the empty places on a blot membrane, so that antibodies or probes stick only to what they are meant to find.
blotto.sourceName: Gene Analysis Techniques (1984), Johnson et al.

acidCasein.text: Casein, milk's main protein, precipitated out of skimmed milk by acid at its isoelectric point, pH 4.6 to 4.7, then washed and dried. Used in foods and industry, dissolved in alkali to make caseinates, and once the base of casein glues.
acidCasein.sourceName: Tetra Pak Dairy Processing Handbook, ch. Cheese (casein section)

rennetCasein.text: Casein set out of skimmed milk with rennet rather than acid, then washed and dried. It was the raw material of casein plastics such as Galalith and Erinoid, hardened with formaldehyde, and is used today in processed and imitation cheese.
rennetCasein.sourceName: Gloucestershire Society for Industrial Archaeology Journal (1999), 'The Centenary of Casein'

caseinate.text: The water-soluble form of casein. Acid casein curd is dissolved in a dilute alkali, usually sodium hydroxide (calcium, potassium and ammonium are also used), and the solution is spray-dried. Sodium caseinate is the most common form, valued as an emulsifier in processed meat, baking and dairy-based foods.
caseinate.sourceName: INFLIBNET (UGC, India): Technology of Milk and Milk Products

caseinGlue.text: Glue made from casein mixed with water, hydrated lime and often caustic soda; with enough lime it resists water. Used in crude form for woodwork since the Middle Ages, made as an industry from the 19th century, and in wide demand for military aircraft from 1916–17.
caseinGlue.sourceName: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Report 280 'Casein Glues' (1930, rev. 1961)

beerLabelGlue.text: A casein-based adhesive long established for labelling glass bottles: it holds the label through condensation and chilling, yet comes off cleanly in the hot caustic wash, so that returnable bottles can be cleaned and refilled.
beerLabelGlue.sourceName: Henkel technical article (2013), Optal XP vs casein label adhesives

caseinPaint.text: Casein paint, occasionally marketed as milk paint, derived from casein, is a fast-drying, water-soluble medium used by artists. It is a paint bound with casein. It can be made from milk and lime, generally with pigment added for color.

galalith.text: Galalith is a synthetic plastic material manufactured by the interaction of casein and formaldehyde. The commercial name is derived from the Ancient Greek words gala and lithos. It is odourless, hard, resists humidity to a certain degree, is antistatic, also an electrical insulator and virtually nonflammable. It was produced under a plethora of other commercial names such as aladdinite, Casolith and lactoloid.

lanital.text: Milk fiber or milk wool is a type of Azlon, a regenerated protein fiber based on the casein protein found in milk. There are several trade names for milk-casein-based fibers, including Lanital, Fibrolane and Aralac.

caseinHydrolysate.text: Casein broken down into short peptides, used as the protein in 'extensively hydrolysed' infant formulas for babies allergic to cow's-milk protein. Mead Johnson's Nutramigen is the long-standing reference product. Its peptides are mostly under about 2 kDa, too small to trigger the antibodies that cause an allergic reaction.

cppAcp.text: Casein phosphopeptide–amorphous calcium phosphate: a material made from the milk protein casein that holds calcium and phosphate in a form the body can use. It is sold in products such as Tooth Mousse and MI Paste, under the Recaldent name, and deposits these minerals on tooth enamel to help repair early white-spot decay.

Kalvdans.text: Kalvdans is a classical Scandinavian dessert. It is made from unpasteurized colostrum milk, the first milk produced by a cow after giving birth.

Ábrystir.text: Icelandic colostrum pudding: the first milk after a cow calves, often mixed half and half with whole milk, heated gently over simmering water until it sets firm. Eaten hot or cold, often with cinnamon sugar.

Junnu.text: Kharvas, also known as Junnu, or Ginnu, is an Indian milk pudding made from cow or buffalo colostrum, the first form of milk produced within one or two days of giving birth. It is prepared by steaming a mix of colostrum, milk, and jaggery or sugar until it coagulates into a jiggling solid. Cardamom, saffron, nutmeg or sesame is added for flavoring. The dish is rich in protein.

Kharvas.text: Kharvas, also known as Junnu, or Ginnu, is an Indian milk pudding made from cow or buffalo colostrum, the first form of milk produced within one or two days of giving birth. It is prepared by steaming a mix of colostrum, milk, and jaggery or sugar until it coagulates into a jiggling solid. Cardamom, saffron, nutmeg or sesame is added for flavoring. The dish is rich in protein.

ATryn.text: ATryn is the brand name of the anticoagulant antithrombin manufactured by the Massachusetts-based U.S. company rEVO Biologics. It is made from the milk of goats that have been genetically modified to produce human antithrombin, a plasma protein with anticoagulant properties. Microinjection was used to insert human antithrombin genes into the cell nucleus of their embryos. ATryn is the first medicine produced using genetically engineered animals. GTC states that one genetically modified goat can produce the same amount of antithrombin in a year as 90,000 blood donations. GTC chose goats for the process because they reproduce more rapidly than cattle and produce more protein than rabbits or mice.

Ruconest.text: Conestat alfa, a recombinant human C1-esterase inhibitor taken from the milk of rabbits given the human gene. It was approved in the EU in 2010 and is injected to treat acute attacks of hereditary angioedema. Because it contains traces of rabbit protein, it must not be given to people allergic to rabbits.

Cornish clotted cream.text: Clotted cream made in Cornwall from Cornish milk, a protected designation of origin: at least 55 % fat, cream to golden yellow, with a thick crust formed by scalding. Eaten with jam on scones in a cream tea.
Cornish clotted cream.sourceName: UK PDO product specification, Cornish Clotted Cream (Defra)

Kaymak.text: Kaymak, also known as qishta or sarshir, is a creamy dairy food similar to clotted cream, made from the milk of water buffalo, cows, sheep, or goats in Central Asia, most Turkic regions on the Eurasian Steppe, the Caucasus, Turkey, most Balkan countries, the Levant, Iran and Iraq.

Malai.text: Malai is a type of clotted cream, originating from the Indian subcontinent. It is used in the cuisine of the Indian subcontinent, especially in sweets from the Indian subcontinent. It is made by heating non-homogenized whole milk to about 80 °C (180 °F) for about one hour and then cooling it. A thick yellowish layer of fat and coagulated proteins forms on the surface, which is skimmed off.

Urum.text: Mongolian öröm: the thick skin of cream that forms on top of boiled milk, usually cow or yak milk. The milk is heated slowly and ladled to aerate it, so the fat rises to form a skin. The pot is left in a cool place for 12–24 hours, then the skin is lifted off in a folded sheet.

Lemon posset.text: A cold dessert of cream heated with sugar and set with lemon juice, dating from the late 19th century: a revival of the name of the old posset, a hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale.

Syllabub.text: Syllabub refers to both a pudding and a beverage, both made by curdling cream or milk with an acid such as wine or cider. Both dishes were popular in British cuisine from the 16th to the 19th centuries. The holiday punch, sweet and frothy, was often considered a ladies' drink.

Gelato.text: Gelato refers to a specific type of ice cream of Italian origin. In Italian, gelato is the common word for all types of ice cream. Artisanal gelato in Italy generally contains 6–9% butterfat, which is lower than other styles of frozen dessert. Gelato typically contains 20–35% air, and more flavoring than other types of frozen desserts, giving it an intense flavor with creamy, smooth texture, density and richness that distinguishes it from other ice creams.

Soft serve.text: Soft serve, also known as soft ice cream, is a frozen dessert and variety of ice cream, similar to conventional ice cream, but softer and less dense due to more air being introduced during freezing. Soft serve has been sold commercially since the late 1930s in the United States.

Frozen custard.text: Frozen custard is a frozen dessert that is a type of ice cream made with egg yolks in addition to cream and sweetener, and an additional flavoring such as cocoa, vanilla, or fruit such as strawberries or peaches. It is usually kept at a warmer temperature compared to ice cream, and typically has a denser and thicker consistency.

Dondurma.text: Dondurma is the Turkish word for ice cream. Maraş dondurması or dövme dondurma is a Turkish variety associated with the city and province of Kahramanmaraş, known for its elastic texture and distinctive preparation. Traditional Maraş dondurması is made using goat's milk, salep, and sugar.

Makhan.text: The butter of the Indian subcontinent churned from dahi, set yoghurt made from whole milk or malai, rather than from fresh cream, traditionally by hand in an earthen pot. Eaten fresh, or heated slowly into desi ghee.
Makhan.sourceName: Journal of Food Science and Technology (2020)

Kibe.text: Ethiopian butter churned from ergo, naturally soured whole milk, in a clay pot or bottle gourd, then washed in cold water. Spiced and clarified, it becomes niter kibbeh.
Kibe.sourceName: Livestock Research for Rural Development 19(7) (2007), Yilma et al.

Zebda.text: The raw fresh butter of Morocco (zebda beldiya), churned from rayeb, raw milk left to sour for one to three days in an earthen jar or goatskin bag; the liquid left behind is lben. Salted and fermented, it becomes smen.
Zebda.sourceName: Benkirane et al., J. Microbiology, Biotechnology and Food Sciences (2022)

Lben.text: The Moroccan and Algerian fermented buttermilk. Raw milk is left to sour on its own at room temperature until it sets, then churned to separate raw butter (zebda beldia). The tangy skimmed liquid that remains is lben. It keeps only a few days.

Chaas.text: Chaas is a curd-based drink popular across the Indian subcontinent.

Rob.text: The sour buttermilk of Sudan: milk is left to sour for about a day, then shaken in a gourd until the butter (fursa) separates, and the liquid left over is drunk as it is.
Rob.sourceName: FAO, The technology of traditional milk products in developing countries

Arera.text: The buttermilk left in Ethiopia after kibe is churned from ergo, soured milk: drunk as it is, or heated to make ayib cheese.
Arera.sourceName: Food Science & Nutrition (2024), review of Ethiopian fermented milk products

Dickmilch.text: German soured milk that has set thick enough to spoon, made from milk with mesophilic lactic cultures and not heated after fermentation. The standard variety has at least 3.5 % fat.

Filmjölk.text: Filmjölk, also known as fil, is a traditional fermented milk product from Sweden, and a common dairy product within most of the Nordic countries. It is made by fermenting cow's milk with a variety of bacteria from the species Lactococcus lactis and Leuconostoc mesenteroides. The bacteria metabolize lactose, the sugar naturally found in milk, into lactic acid, which means people who are lactose intolerant can tolerate it better than other dairy products. The acid gives filmjölk a sour taste and causes proteins in the milk, mainly casein, to coagulate, thus thickening the final product. The bacteria also produce a limited amount of diacetyl, a compound with a buttery flavor, which gives filmjölk its characteristic taste.

Prostokvasha.text: The Russian soured milk. Traditionally milk was left to sour on its own or started with some ready soured milk. Factory versions use pure cultures that define the type: mesophilic lactococci for ordinary prostokvasha, thermophilic streptococci with Lactobacillus bulgaricus for the Mechnikov kind.

Clabber.text: Clabber is a type of soured milk. It is produced by allowing unpasteurized milk to turn sour (ferment) at a specific humidity and temperature. Over time, the milk thickens or curdles into a yogurt-like consistency with a strong, sour flavor. According to Joy of Cooking, "Clabber... is milk that has soured to the stage of a firm curd but not to a separation of the whey."

Piimä.text: The Finnish soured milk drink, tart and thicker than milk. Pasteurised milk is fermented at 18–24 °C for 15–24 hours. It is also the buttermilk left from churning cultured cream (kirnupiimä). Western Finland traditionally made a stringy long piimä, eastern Finland a curdled one.

Långfil.text: A Swedish fermented milk with a cohesive, stretchy ('long') texture and mild sourness. It is cultured slowly at low temperature with Lactococcus lactis subsp. cremoris strains that make exopolysaccharides. It was traditional in northern and central Sweden and western Finland, where a dried cloth soaked in old fil carried the culture.

Viili.text: Viili (Finnish) or Fil (Swedish) is a mesophilic fermented milk product found in the Nordic countries, particularly Finland and Sweden. Viili is similar to yoghurt or kefir, but when left unmixed, its texture is malleable, or "long". The metabolism of the bacteria used in the fermentation also gives viili a slightly different taste.

Tätmjölk.text: A ropy soured milk of central and northern Sweden, traditionally made long and stringy with butterwort (Pinguicula, in Swedish tätört) or with a starter kept from an earlier batch. On summer farms (fäbodar) it kept for months.

Varenets.text: Varenets, sometimes anglicised as stewler or simmeler, is a fermented milk product that is popular in Russia. Similar to ryazhenka, it is made by adding sour cream (smetana) to baked milk.

Bioghurt.text: A mild yoghurt culture and product name from Germany, introduced in 1956: Streptococcus thermophilus with Lactobacillus acidophilus in place of the sharper Lactobacillus bulgaricus, so the yoghurt sours less. Its sister culture Biogarde adds bifidobacteria.

Actimel.text: Actimel is a probiotic yoghurt-type drink produced by the French company Danone.

Yakult.text: Yakult is a Japanese sweetened probiotic milk beverage fermented with the bacteria strain Lacticaseibacillus casei Shirota. It is sold by Yakult Honsha, based in Tokyo. The name "Yakult" was coined from jahurto, an Esperanto word meaning "yogurt".

Acidophilus milk.text: Milk fermented with Lactobacillus acidophilus. Interest in it goes back about 80 years, to when it was used to treat intestinal infections. Later studies looked at lactose digestion, cholesterol and cancer, and concluded that any benefit depends on careful choice of strain.

Dahi.text: Dahi is a traditional yogurt or fermented milk product originating from and popular throughout the Indian subcontinent. It is usually prepared from cows' milk, and sometimes buffalo milk or goat milk. The word curd is used in Indian English to refer to homemade yogurt, while the term yogurt refers to the pasteurized commercial variety known as "heat-treated fermented milk".

Tarag.text: Mongolian yoghurt, made from cow's, yak's, goat's or sheep's milk. Eaten as it is, dried into aaruul, or, made from cow's or yak's milk, distilled into shimiin arkhi.
Tarag.sourceName: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

Matsoni.text: Matzoon or matsoni is a fermented milk product of Armenian origin found in Armenia and Georgia. The Caspian Sea yogurt commercialized in Japan is said to be the same type of yogurt as matzoon, but a comparison of microbiota and viscosity found that the two are entirely different. Georgian matsoni has been a protected geographical indication in Georgia since 24 January 2012.

Labneh.text: The Levantine strained yogurt, taken further than Greek yogurt. In Lebanon and other Middle Eastern countries, set yogurt is drained in cloth bags until it reaches about 23–25% solids and 9–11% fat. Commercial labneh keeps for two to three weeks in the fridge.

Chakka.text: Indian yoghurt strained in muslin until it is thick and semi-solid. Sweetened and spiced with cardamom and saffron, it becomes shrikhand.

Suzma.text: Strained yoghurt of Central Asia, drained from qatiq until it is thick; in Turkey it is süzme yoğurt, or kese yoğurdu, 'bag yoghurt'. Dried further, it becomes qurut.

Doogh.text: Doogh is a cold and savoury Persian drink. It is made with fermented milk. Unlike ayran, a yoghurt drink of Turkish origin, doogh is not diluted yogurt. According to the Iranian Ministry of Food Standards, doogh "is a drink resulting from lactic fermentation of milk whose dry matter is standardized by diluting yogurt or buttermilk ."

Tan.text: The Armenian yogurt drink: matsun (Armenian yogurt) thinned with water and salted, sometimes with herbs. It is drunk across the Caucasus mountains, and industrial versions have been sold since the 1990s.

Mastaw.text: The Kurdish yogurt drink, also called ava mast: yogurt and salt mixed with water. Yogurt (mast) is the most widely eaten fermented dairy product among Kurds.

Salted lassi.text: Lassi is a yogurt–based beverage with a smoothie-like consistency. The word 'lassi' for the drink is a borrowing from Hindi, first attested in 1882; its ultimate origin is unclear, and has been suggested as derived ultimately from Sanskrit lasya (stickiness) or rasah (juice).

Kashk.text: Iran's kashk: yoghurt churned with water to take off the butter, the defatted liquid boiled, drained in linen bags, salted, shaped and sun-dried into hard, protein-rich balls, which are later ground and soaked back into liquid kashk.
Kashk.sourceName: Say, Soltani & Güzeler, Pamukkale Univ. J. Eng. Sci. (2015)

Qurut.text: The dried fermented-milk cheese of the Kazakhs and other Central Asian nomads; the name comes from the Turkic word for ‘dry’. Milk is soured with yoghurt from an earlier batch, boiled, and the curd pressed in cloth, salted, rolled into small balls and sun-dried for up to two weeks. It keeps for over a year.

Chortan.text: The Armenian name (չորթան) for dried tan, the buttermilk left after butter is churned from matsun; dried into a hard, keeping food like the qurut of Central Asia.

Aaruul.text: Mongolian dried curd, a long-standing portable food of herding families. Most is made from the yoghurt of cows or yaks, although any livestock milk or yoghurt can be used. The curd is spread on the sloping roof of the ger to dry in the sun, then shaped. Sugar is sometimes added. Once hard, it keeps for a long time.

Choormog.text: The Mongolian name (khoormog) for fermented camel's milk, left to sour naturally and made by camel-herding households, mostly in the Gobi, as airag is from mare's milk.
Choormog.sourceName: FAO, One Country One Priority Product: Mongolia

Shubat.text: Chal, also shubat or khoormog, is a Turkic and Mongolic beverage of fermented camel milk, sparkling white with a sour flavor, popular in Central Asia — particularly in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. In Kazakhstan the drink is known as shubat, and is a staple summer food. Due to preparation requirements and perishable nature, chal has proved difficult to export. Agaran is collected from the surface of chal.

Gariss.text: Fermented camel milk made by camel herders in the pastoral areas of Sudan. Traditionally it ferments while the herd is on the move: the jolting of the camel's walk shakes the milk in its bag. Herders start each batch with soured product kept back from earlier batches instead of a pure culture.

Suusac.text: Fermented camel milk from the pastoralist herds of northern Kenya, also spelled suusa. Raw camel milk is left to sour by itself, with no starter culture. Its containers are first fumigated with smoke from particular woods, which helps it keep and gives it a smoky taste. Women do the processing.
Suusac.sourceName: African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition and Development (2013)

Dhanaan.text: Fermented camel's milk of the Somali herders of eastern Ethiopia, left to sour on its own in a clean or smoked container; the smoke, from woods such as wild olive, helps it keep.
Dhanaan.sourceName: Seifu, Livestock Research for Rural Development (2007)

Shimiin arkhi.text: Mongolian milk spirit, distilled from fermented cow's or yak's milk (tarag) in a still of a cauldron, a wooden barrel and a second pot of cold water, to about 10–16 % alcohol. Rarer than airag, it is opened with an offering to the spirits.
Shimiin arkhi.sourceName: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

Araka.text: The milk spirit of the Khakas of southern Siberia, distilled from airan, soured milk, and formerly also from kumis.

Tarasun.text: The Buryat milk spirit, distilled from soured mare's or cow's milk; poured as an offering at festivals and shamanic rites as well as drunk.

Araga.text: The Tuvan milk spirit, distilled from khoitpak, a soured milk drink, and also from kumis; made only in summer, when there was milk to spare.

Artz.text: Arkhi distilled a second time, stronger than the first, at around 30 % alcohol: in Mongolian, arz.
Artz.sourceName: Bianquis, Les alcools de lait en Mongolie (OCHA, 2004)

Khorz.text: Arkhi distilled a third time, stronger still, after artz.
Khorz.sourceName: Mongolian Academy of Sciences dictionary (mongoltoli.mn), entry арз

Harzer.text: A German sour-milk cheese from the northern Harz foothills, though most is now made elsewhere. Crumbly, low-fat sour-milk quark from cow’s milk is shaped and coated with red-smear bacteria, ripening within days into a pungent cheese with under 10% fat in dry matter, often seasoned with caraway.

Olmützer Quargel.text: Olomoucké tvarůžky, also known as olomoucké syrečky or tvargle, English: Olomouc cheese, Olomouc curd cheese) is a ripened soft cheese made in Loštice, Olomouc Region, Czech Republic. The cheese is very easy to recognize by its strong scent, distinctive pungent taste and yellowish colour. It is named after the city of Olomouc where it was originally sold.

Tiroler Graukäse.text: Tyrolean grey cheese is a strongly flavoured, rennet-free cows-milk acid-curd quark made in the Tyrolean Alp valleys, Austria. It owes its name to the grey mold that usually grows on its rind. It is extremely low in fat and has a powerful penetrating smell. The cheese produced in Austria is registered as protected designation of origin (PDO), Austria generally indicated in German as g.U. under the official name Tiroler Graukäse. The registration of the PDO states that its production has been a significant element of Tyrolean peasant gastronomy for centuries. Graukäse produced in Italy is protected by a prodotti agroalimentari tradizionali (PAT) designation. Graukäse making became widespread on farms due to the simplicity of making and the availability of low-fat milk after the fat had been taken for use in butter making.

Handkäse.text: Handkäse is a German regional sour milk cheese and is a culinary specialty of Frankfurt am Main, Offenbach am Main, Darmstadt, Langen, and other parts of southern Hesse. It gets its name from the traditional way of producing it: forming it with one's own hands.

Mainzer.text: A German sour milk cheese named after Mainz and grouped with Harzer in the German cheese regulations: small low-fat cheeses of 25–125 g, made from sour milk quark and ripened with a yellow or red smear.

Rubing.text: Rubing is a firm, acid-set, non-melting, fresh goat milk farmer cheese made in the Yunnan Province of China by people of the Bai and Sani minorities. Its Bai name is youdbap, meaning "goat's milk".

Rasgulla.text: Rasgulla is a syrupy dessert popular in the eastern part of India & South Asia. It is made from ball-shaped dumplings of chhena dough cooked in light sugar syrup until the syrup permeates the dumplings.

Sandesh.text: Sandesh is a Bengali dessert, originating from the undivided Bengal region in the eastern part of the Indian subcontinent, created with milk and sugar. Some recipes of sandesh call for the use of chhena or paneer instead of milk itself. Some people in the region of Dhaka make a variety of sandesh called pranahara which is softer and made with mawa and yogurt. Basirhat is known for its kachagolla sandesh. Historically, it can be seen that the culture of making this kachagolla in Basirhat is about 400 years old. The Gupo or Gufo style of sandesh from Guptipara is considered by some to be the "first branded sweet of Bengal".

Rasmalai.text: Ras malai, also known as rasamalei or roshmalai, is a dessert that originated in the Bengal region of the Indian subcontinent. The dessert is called roshmalai in Bengali, ras malai in Hindi, and rasa malei in Odia. It is popular in India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

Wagashi.text: A soft cheese from northern Benin, made by women and mostly by the Peulh (Fulani). Fresh whole cow's milk is heated and curdled with an extract of the Sodom apple plant (Calotropis procera), whose enzyme does the work of rennet. The curd drains in small colanders. Some cheeses are dyed red with sorghum.

Dangke.text: Dangke is a type of cottage cheese produced in Enrekang, South Sulawesi, Indonesia, especially in Enrekang, Baraka, Anggeraja, and Alla districts. Dangke is processed by boiling fresh cattle or buffalo milk with sliced papaya leaves, stems, or unripe papaya fruits. Dangke is typically soaked in a brine solution overnight before being wrapped with banana leaves for masking the bitter taste caused by the addition of papaya leaves.

Ginger milk curd.text: Ginger milk curd, also known as ginger-juice milk curd, ginger milk pudding or simply ginger milk, is a Chinese dessert originating from Shawan Ancient Town, Panyu District, Guangzhou in the Guangdong Province of southern China. The main ingredients are ginger, milk, and sugar. Water buffalo milk is traditionally used.

Queso fresco.text: Mexico's most popular fresh cheese, also widely eaten in the United States. Skimmed or partly skimmed milk is set with rennet at about 38 °C, and the curd is finely milled before salting, which makes the cheese crumbly. It is pressed only by its own weight, is not ripened and has a short shelf life.
Queso fresco.sourceName: Temas Selectos de Ingeniería de Alimentos (2012)

Panela.text: Queso panela is a fresh cheese common in Mexico made from pasteurized cow's milk. It is also known as queso canasta or queso de la canasta. It is derived from the Greek word for basket cheese. The cheese also has similarities to the Indian cheese paneer.

Robiola.text: Robiola is an Italian soft-ripened cheese of the stracchino family. It is from the Langhe region and made with varying proportions of cow's, goat's, and sheep's milk. One theory is that the cheese gets its name from the comune (municipality) of Robbio, in the province of Pavia; another that the name comes from the word rubeole (ruddy) because of the color of the seasoned rind.

Tomino.text: A small cheese from Piedmont, made from cow's or goat's milk or a mix of both. The milk is warmed with rennet and the curd is broken up finely and drained. Eaten fresh, it is soft, moist and white. Matured ones get a thin rind and a stronger smell and are often warmed in a pan or on soapstone.

Bel Paese.text: An industrial Italian cheese created by Egidio Galbani in 1906 and named after Antonio Stoppani’s book Il Bel Paese, whose author’s portrait appears on the wrapper. It is made from pasteurised cow’s milk and ripened for six to eight weeks, giving a mild, creamy cheese with 45–50% fat in dry matter.

Butterkäse.text: Butterkäse is a semi-soft, cow's milk cheese moderately popular in Germanic Europe, and occasionally seen in the rest of the cheese-eating world. Although primarily produced in Germany, some Butterkäse is produced in Wisconsin.

Saint-Paulin.text: Saint Paulin is a creamy, mild, semi-soft French cheese made from pasteurized cow's milk, originally made by Trappist monks at Saint Paulin. It is a buttery cheese, but firm enough for slicing. Saint Paulin is similar to Havarti and Esrom, and is suited to serving as a table or dessert cheese; it is often served with fruit and light wine. Genuine Saint Paulin has an edible yellow-orange rind. It is ripened in a round loaf with slightly protruding sides, and matures in about four weeks.

Stracchino.text: Stracchino, also known as crescenza, is an Italian cow's milk cheese typical of the regions of Lombardy, Tuscany, Veneto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, and Liguria. It is eaten very young, has no rind and has a very soft, creamy texture and normally a mild, slightly acidic flavour. It is normally square in shape.

Cuartirolo.text: An Argentine soft cheese defined in the national food code: whole or standardised milk is soured with lactic cultures and set with rennet, and the curd is moulded, pressed, salted and ripened for at least 20 days. The result is a high-moisture, fatty cheese with a soft, slightly acidic, white-to-yellowish paste.

Manchego.text: Manchego is a cheese made in the La Mancha region of Spain from the milk of sheep of the Manchega breed. It is aged between 60 days and 2 years.

Tilsiter.text: Tilsit cheese or Tilsiter cheese is a pale yellow semihard smear-ripened cheese, created in the mid-19th century by Prussian-Swiss settlers, the Westphal family, from the Emmental valley. The original buildings from the cheese plant still exist in Sovetsk, Russia, formerly Tilsit, on the Neman River, in the former German province of East Prussia.

Havarti.text: Havarti or cream Havarti is a semisoft Danish cow's milk cheese. It can be sliced, grilled, or melted.

Monterey Jack.text: Monterey Jack, sometimes shortened to Jack, is a Californian white, semi-hard cheese made using cow's milk, with a mild flavor and slight sweetness. Originating in Monterey, on the Central Coast of California, the cheese has been called "a vestige of Spanish rule in the early nineteenth century, deriving from a Franciscan monastic style of farmer's cheese".

Morbier.text: Morbier is a semi-soft cows' milk cheese of France named after the small village of Morbier in Franche-Comté. It is ivory colored, soft and slightly elastic, and is immediately recognizable by the distinctive thin black layer separating it horizontally in the middle. It has a yellowish, sticky rind.

Parmigiano Reggiano.text: Parmesan is an Italian hard, granular cheese produced from cow's milk and aged at least 12 months. It is a grana-type cheese, along with Grana Padano, the historic Granone Lodigiano, and others.

Grana Padano.text: Grana Padano is an Italian cheese originating in the Po Valley. It is similar to Parmesan but with less strict regulations governing its production. This hard, crumbly-textured cheese is made with unpasteurized cows' milk that is semi-skimmed. To preserve the authenticity of the manufacturing processes and raw materials used to make this cheese, Grana Padano was registered as a denominazione di origine controllata (DOC) in 1955, and as a European Union protected designation of origin (PDO) in 1996. Outside of the EU, its name is protected in several other countries on the basis of the Lisbon Agreement and bilateral agreements.

Pecorino Romano.text: Pecorino romano is a hard, salty Italian cheese made from sheep milk, often used for grating over pasta or other dishes. The name pecorino means 'ovine' or 'of sheep' in Italian; the name of the cheese, although protected, is a description rather than a brand: [formaggio] pecorino romano means 'sheep's [cheese] of Rome'.

Sbrinz.text: Sbrinz is a very hard cheese produced in Central Switzerland. It is often used as grated cheese in Swiss cuisine, although it is also eaten in small pieces. The cheese is produced in only 42 dairies in Central Switzerland. Only local cow's milk is used when producing this cheese. It is kept in the region until ready for consumption. It is the hardest of Swiss cheeses together with Berner Hobelkäse.

Mahón.text: Mahón cheese is a soft to hard white cheese made from cows' milk, named after the town and natural port of Mahón, on the island of Menorca off the Mediterranean coast of Spain. Menorca is known for its cheese production.
